steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI/NLP paper that proposes a way to evaluate the creativity of short stories, adapted from the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, and uses it to compare stories by professional writers with stories generated by LLMs, and to test whether LLMs can act as the evaluators. Include the research questions with headline findings and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs as creative writing assistants; evaluating creativity is hard
- From TTCT (creativity as process) to TTCW (creativity as product) via the Consensual Assessment Technique
- Benchmark of expert and LLM stories, expert assessment, and research questions RQ1-RQ3
- LLMs as assessors
- Contributions

  - direct TTCT application not possible across creative domains (cite), but dimensions adaptable (cite)
  - TTCT + Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) (cite) -> Torrance Tests for Creative Writing (TTCW) (Section 3 Design Principle 1 and 2; Figure 1 Step 1)
  - CAT: most valid assessment of creativity = collective judgment of experts in the field
  - formative study (Section 4): 8 creative writing experts propose measures for short fictional stories aligned with four dimensions

  - new set of 10 experts (CAT), 14 tests per story, 3 evaluations per story (Figure 1 Step 3)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recent work has looked at using large language models (LLMs) as assistants in creative writing tasks, from stories to screenplays. One important aspect of this research is to look at how capable LLMs are, both at generating creative content and at assessing whether a piece of writing is creative, with the final goal of informing interaction design. But it is challenging to evaluate the creativity of a piece of writing objectively.

We propose a protocol to evaluate creativity as product, and we ground it in a widely accepted protocol that evaluates creativity as process, which is the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT). TTCT is based on Guilford's work on divergent thinking, and it measures creativity as a process by testing how well participants deal with unusual uses of objects, specific situations or impossibilities. TTCT evaluates four dimensions of creativity: fluency (how many meaningful ideas are produced in reaction to a given stimulus), flexibility (how diverse the categories in the responses are), originality (how unique or novel the answers are) and elaboration (how deep or detailed the responses are). It might not be possible to apply TTCT directly across diverse creative domains, but its four fundamental dimensions have proven adaptable. So, based on TTCT and using the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT), we design the Torrance Tests for Creative Writing (TTCW) to evaluate creativity as product (Section 3 Design Principle 1 and 2; Figure 1 Step 1). The Consensual Assessment Technique says that the most valid assessment of the creativity of an idea or creation in any field is the collective judgment of experts in that field. So to design TTCW we asked 8 creative writing experts in a formative study (Section 4) to propose creativity measures for evaluating short fictional stories that align with the four Torrance dimensions. This gave 14 binary tests, organized across the four original Torrance dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (Section 4.2).

To validate TTCW empirically as an evaluation protocol for creativity as product (fictional short stories), we build a benchmark of 48 short stories. 12 of the stories are written by professionals, and 36 are written by three top performing LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT4 and Claude 1.3), and the stories have 1400 words on average (Section 5; Figure 1 Step 2). We recruit a new set of 10 experts, again following CAT, to administer the 14 tests of TTCW on each story, and we collect 3 evaluations per story. With this TTCW implementation with experts as assessors (Figure 1 Step 3) we want to answer three research questions:

- RQ1: consistent, reproducible? 2,000+ tests; moderate agreement (Fleiss Kappa 0.41) on average across 14 tests; strong when aggregated (Pearson correlation 0.69) -> TTCW valid
- RQ2: human vs LLM stories; expert stories pass 84.7% on average; LLM stories from 9% (ChatGPT) to 30% (Claude); three to ten times less likely to pass
- RQ3: specializations; GPT4 -> Originality; Claude V1.3 -> Fluency, Flexibility, Elaboration
- LLMs as assessors
  - prior work: LLMs regurgitate pre-training text -> often not truly original (Section 5.6); but maybe feedback to authors
  - TTCW with LLMs as assessors (Section 6; Figure 1 Step 3); each test -> detailed prompt; correlation with experts close to zero
- Contributions
  - TTCT -> TTCW, 14 tests via CAT, four dimensions
  - validation: 48 stories, 10 experts; moderate agreement per test, strong in aggregate
  - LLM generation and assessment findings; release 2,000+ assessments with expert explanations
  - discussion: experts distinguishing AI vs human stories; future writing support tools

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recent work has looked at using large language models (LLMs) as assistants in creative writing tasks, from stories to screenplays. One important aspect of this research is to look at how capable LLMs are, both at generating creative content and at assessing whether a piece of writing is creative, with the final goal of informing interaction design. But it is challenging to evaluate the creativity of a piece of writing objectively.

We propose a protocol to evaluate creativity as product, and we ground it in a widely accepted protocol that evaluates creativity as process, which is the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT). TTCT is based on Guilford's work on divergent thinking, and it measures creativity as a process by testing how well participants deal with unusual uses of objects, specific situations or impossibilities. TTCT evaluates four dimensions of creativity: fluency (how many meaningful ideas are produced in reaction to a given stimulus), flexibility (how diverse the categories in the responses are), originality (how unique or novel the answers are) and elaboration (how deep or detailed the responses are). It might not be possible to apply TTCT directly across diverse creative domains, but its four fundamental dimensions have proven adaptable. So, based on TTCT and using the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT), we design the Torrance Tests for Creative Writing (TTCW) to evaluate creativity as product (Section 3 Design Principle 1 and 2; Figure 1 Step 1). The Consensual Assessment Technique says that the most valid assessment of the creativity of an idea or creation in any field is the collective judgment of experts in that field. So to design TTCW we asked 8 creative writing experts in a formative study (Section 4) to propose creativity measures for evaluating short fictional stories that align with the four Torrance dimensions. This gave 14 binary tests, organized across the four original Torrance dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (Section 4.2).

To validate TTCW empirically as an evaluation protocol for creativity as product (fictional short stories), we build a benchmark of 48 short stories. 12 of the stories are written by professionals, and 36 are written by three top performing LLMs (ChatGPT, GPT4 and Claude 1.3), and the stories have 1400 words on average (Section 5; Figure 1 Step 2). We recruit a new set of 10 experts, again following CAT, to administer the 14 tests of TTCW on each story, and we collect 3 evaluations per story. With this TTCW implementation with experts as assessors (Figure 1 Step 3) we want to answer three research questions:

- RQ1: Is creative evaluation based on TTCW consistent and reproducible? That is, do expert annotators agree when they perform the tests on the same stories? Based on more than 2,000 tests administered by experts, we find that experts reach moderate agreement on average (Fleiss Kappa 0.41) across the 14 TTCW tests, and strong agreement when the tests are aggregated (Pearson correlation 0.69). This confirms that TTCW is valid for evaluating creativity in fictional short stories.

- RQ2: Are human-written stories more likely to pass individual TTCW tests than stories generated by LLMs? If yes, which tests show the biggest gaps? When we analyze the tests, the 12 stories written by experts pass 84.7% of the tests on average. This confirms that an expert story does not have to pass all tests to be considered creative, but experienced writers usually produce artifacts that pass most of the tests. LLM-generated stories pass a lot fewer tests on average, from 9% for ChatGPT stories up to 30% for Claude stories. So LLM-generated stories are three to ten times less likely to pass individual TTCW tests than stories written by experts, and this shows a wide gap in the evaluated creativity of content generated by LLMs.

- RQ3: Which LLMs do better in TTCW evaluation, and do we see specializations, with different LLMs doing better on different Torrance dimensions? Apart from the general gap, because TTCW is granular we can see that individual LLMs have different abilities: GPT4 is more likely to pass tests associated with Originality, and Claude V1.3 is more likely to pass tests in Fluency, Flexibility and Elaboration.

Prior work has argued that because LLMs regurgitate text they saw during pre-training, they are often not able to directly generate a piece of writing that is truly original and creative (see also Section 5.6). But they might be used to give feedback to authors while they are writing. So we do a study of TTCW implementation with LLMs as assessors (Section 6; and Figure 1 Step 3) to find out if LLMs can be used to assess creative writing. We expanded each test into a detailed prompt and measured if the LLM assessments correlate with the expert judgments we collected. Our analysis shows that for the most part LLMs cannot administer the TTCW tests, since the three LLMs we experiment with get correlations with experts that are close to zero.

To summarize, our work makes these contributions:

- We adapt the Torrance Test for Creative Thinking (TTCT), which is a protocol for evaluating creativity as a process, and align it to evaluating creativity as a product, focusing on short stories in particular. Using the Consensual Assessment Technique, we design 14 tests that we call the Torrance Test for Creative Writing (TTCW), based on the four original Torrance dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration.

- We validate TTCW experimentally with an assessment of 48 stories by 10 participants who have expertise in creative writing, and we find that they reach moderate agreement when they administer individual tests and strong agreement when all tests are evaluated in aggregate.

- We study how well LLMs can generate stories that pass/fail the TTCW tests and how reliably they can assess the creativity of stories with the TTCW framework, by correlating them with human judgments. We find that LLM-generated stories are three to ten times less likely to pass TTCW tests than stories written by experts, and that current state-of-the-art LLMs cannot yet reproduce expert assessments when they administer TTCW tests. To enable future research in this fast-evolving domain, we release the large-scale annotation of 2,000+ TTCW assessments, each with a natural language explanation by an expert.

- Finally, we discuss how creative writing experts can tell AI-written stories apart from human-written ones, and how future work can use our evaluation framework to build rich interactive writing support tools.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent work has explored the potential of using large language models (LLMs) as assistants in creative writing tasks, from stories to screenplays [1,2,3,4,5]. An important aspect of this research is investigating LLMs' capabilities both to generate creative content and to assess whether a piece of writing is creative, with the ultimate goal of informing interaction design. We propose a protocol to evaluate creativity as product, grounded in a widely accepted protocol that evaluates creativity as process: the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) [6]. Based on Guilford's work on divergent thinking [7], TTCT measures creativity as a process by testing participants' abilities to deal with unusual uses of objects, specific situations, or impossibilities. TTCT evaluates four dimensions of creativity: fluency (the sheer volume of meaningful ideas produced in reaction to a given stimulus), flexibility (the diversity of categories within the responses), originality (the uniqueness or novelty of answers) and elaboration (the depth or granularity of details within the responses). While TTCT might not be directly applicable across diverse creative domains [8,9], its four fundamental dimensions have proven adaptable [10,11,12]. Thus, based on TTCT and using the Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) [8], we design the Torrance Tests for Creative Writing (TTCW) to evaluate creativity as product (Section 3 Design Principle 1 and 2; Figure 1 Step 1). To design TTCW, we therefore asked 8 creative writing experts in a formative study (Section 4) to propose creativity measures, aligned with the four Torrance dimensions, for evaluating short fictional stories. This resulted in 14 binary tests organized across the four original Torrance dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (Section 4.2).

To empirically validate TTCW as an evaluation protocol for creativity as product (fictional short stories), we build a benchmark of 48 short stories: 12 written by professionals and 36 by three top performing LLMs (ChatGPT [13], GPT4 [14] and Claude 1.3 [15]), with 1400 words on average per story (Section 5; Figure 1 Step 2). We recruit a new set of 10 experts, again following CAT, to administer the 14 TTCW tests on each story, collecting 3 evaluations per story. With this TTCW implementation using experts as assessors (Figure 1 Step 3), we aim to answer three research questions:

- RQ1: Is TTCW-based creative evaluation consistent and reproducible? In other words, do expert annotators agree when they perform tests on the same stories? Based on a total of 2,000+ expert-administered tests, we find that experts reach moderate agreement on average (Fleiss Kappa 0.41) across the 14 TTCW tests, and strong agreement on the aggregated tests (Pearson correlation 0.69). This confirms the validity of TTCW for evaluating creativity in fictional short stories.

- RQ2: Are human-written stories more likely to pass individual TTCW tests than LLM-generated stories? If so, which tests show the most significant gaps? Our analysis shows that the 12 expert-written stories pass an average of 84.7% of the tests, confirming that although an expert story need not pass all tests to be deemed creative, experienced writers typically produce artifacts that pass most of the tests. LLM-generated stories, by comparison, pass far fewer tests on average, from 9% for ChatGPT-generated stories up to 30% for Claude-generated stories. In other words, LLM-generated stories are three to ten times less likely to pass individual TTCW tests than expert-written stories, revealing a wide gap in the evaluated creativity of LLM-generated content.

- RQ3: Which LLMs perform better in TTCW evaluation, and do we observe specializations, with different LLMs performing better on different Torrance dimensions? Beyond the general gap, the granularity of TTCW reveals that individual LLMs differ in their abilities: GPT4 is more likely to pass tests associated with Originality, and Claude V1.3 is more likely to pass tests in Fluency, Flexibility and Elaboration.

Prior work [4] has argued that because LLMs regurgitate text seen during pre-training, they are often unable to directly generate a truly original and creative piece of writing (see also Section 5.6). However, they might be useful for providing feedback to authors during the writing process [16]. We therefore study a TTCW implementation with LLMs as assessors (Section 6; and Figure 1 Step 3) to understand whether LLMs can be used to assess creative writing. We expanded each test into a detailed prompt and measured whether LLM assessments correlate with the expert judgments we collected. Our analysis reveals that, for the most part, LLMs are not capable of administering the TTCW tests: the three LLMs we experiment with achieve correlations with experts close to zero.

In summary, our work makes the following contributions:

- We adapt the Torrance Test for Creative Thinking (TTCT), a protocol for evaluating creativity as a process, to the evaluation of creativity as a product, focusing particularly on short stories. Using the Consensual Assessment Technique, we design 14 tests, called the Torrance Test for Creative Writing (TTCW), based on the four original Torrance dimensions of fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration.

- We experimentally validate TTCW through an assessment of 48 stories by 10 participants with expertise in creative writing, finding that they reach moderate agreement when administering individual tests and strong agreement when evaluating all tests in aggregate.

- We study the abilities of LLMs to generate stories that pass/fail the TTCW tests, and their ability to reliably assess the creativity of stories with the TTCW framework, through correlation with human judgments. We find that LLM-generated stories are three to ten times less likely to pass TTCW tests than expert-written stories, and that current state-of-the-art LLMs are not yet capable of reproducing expert assessments when administering TTCW tests. To enable future research in this fast-evolving domain, we release the large-scale annotation of 2,000+ TTCW assessments, each accompanied by a natural language expert explanation.

- Finally, we discuss how creative writing experts can distinguish between AI- and human-written stories, and how future work can use our evaluation framework to build rich interactive writing support tools.
